report.source_text: Serial MRI brain scans at presentation (A–C), 3 months (D–F) and 6 months (G–I) following initial presentation in a child with Baló’s concentric sclerosis. The initial MRI with contrast demonstrated a T2 hyperintense abnormality with central hypointense ring-like focus (A); alternating layers of high and low signal intensity giving it an ‘onion bulb’ appearance. There was central concentric contrast enhancement (B). At 3 months, the extent of the abnormality (D) and the area of contrast enhancement (E) had increased. At 6 months, the abnormality (G) and the contrast enhancement (H) had resolved. The abnormality showed central diffusion restriction with unrestricted diffusion in the periphery (C). The area of diffusion restriction increased in size at 3 months (F) and disappeared by 6 months (I).

clinician.final_diagnosis: Histopathological examination confirmed a demyelinating inflammatory lesion
clinician.trajectory_summary: An asymptomatic school-aged boy presented with incidental concern for papilloedema. Initial non-enhanced head CT revealed a well-demarcated hyperdense lesion in the left posterior frontal lobe with surrounding oedema. MRI brain at presentation showed a T2 hyperintense lesion with an 'onion bulb' appearance, central concentric contrast enhancement, and central diffusion restriction, suggestive of Baló’s concentric sclerosis. At 3 months, repeat MRI showed an increase in the lesion's size, enhancement, and diffusion restriction, prompting a biopsy to exclude a tumor. Histopathological examination confirmed a demyelinating inflammatory lesion. The patient was managed conservatively, and follow-up MRI at 6 months showed resolution of the abnormality, contrast enhancement, and diffusion restriction. He remained asymptomatic with continuing involution of the lesion at 12 months and was stable and asymptomatic, untreated, with further resolution and no new lesions at 4 years.

The increase in lesion size and change in signal characteristics at 3 months led to the decision to biopsy to exclude a tumor.
At 6 months, the abnormality, contrast enhancement, and diffusion restriction resolved.

The patient remained asymptomatic with continuing involution of the lesion at 12 months and was stable and asymptomatic, untreated, with further resolution of the lesion and no new lesions at 4 years.
